claim: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is the sole and selective gateway for nuclear transport.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is the sole and selective gateway for nuclear transport, and its dysfunction has been associated with many diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the function of NPCs.

claim: NPC dysfunction has been associated with many diseases.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is the sole and selective gateway for nuclear transport, and its dysfunction has been associated with many diseases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Beck and Hurt, 2017 in the Introduction section.

claim: The metazoan NPC subcomplex RanBP2 consists of RanBP2 (Nup358), RanGAP1-SUMO1, and Ubc9.
source: The metazoan NPC subcomplex RanBP2, which consists of RanBP2 (Nup358), RanGAP1-SUMO1, and Ubc9, regulates the assembly and function of the NPC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the RanBP2 subcomplex, supported by multiple citations in the Introduction.

claim: The RanBP2 subcomplex regulates the assembly and function of the NPC.
source: The metazoan NPC subcomplex RanBP2, which consists of RanBP2 (Nup358), RanGAP1-SUMO1, and Ubc9, regulates the assembly and function of the NPC.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies in the Introduction section.

claim: TCR stimulation induces PKC-θ translocation to the nuclear envelope.
source: By biochemically isolating the NE, we observed that anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 antibody (Ab) costimulation or stimulation with APCs that were pulsed with a superantigen, staphylococcal enterotoxin E (SEE), promoted PKC-θ translocation to the NE fraction (Figure 1A,B, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B demonstrating PKC-θ in the NE fraction after stimulation.

claim: TCR stimulation promotes PKC-θ translocation to the plasma membrane.
source: Consistent with previous findings, TCR stimulation also promoted PKC-θ translocation to the plasma membrane (PM) fraction (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A,B and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: After 15 min of stimulation, >20% of total PKC-θ was localized 100 nm or less from the NE.
source: Quantitation showed that after 15 min of stimulation, >20% of total PKC-θ was localized 100 nm or less from the NE and >30% of total PKC-θ was localized 100 nm or less from the PM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After 15 min of stimulation, >30% of total PKC-θ was localized 100 nm or less from the PM.
source: Quantitation showed that after 15 min of stimulation, >20% of total PKC-θ was localized 100 nm or less from the NE and >30% of total PKC-θ was localized 100 nm or less from the PM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TCR stimulation significantly increases PKC-θ colocalization with NPCs.
source: Staining with an anti-PKC-θ Ab and a monoclonal Ab (Mab414) that recognizes a subset of NPC proteins revealed that stimulation significantly increased PKC-θ colocalization with NPCs (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: TCR costimulation increases PKC-θ binding to NPCs in primary human T cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation (IP) with Mab414 showed that costimulation increased PKC-θ binding to NPCs in primary human T cells (Figure 1E) and in Jurkat T cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TCR costimulation increases PKC-θ binding to NPCs in Jurkat T cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation (IP) with Mab414 showed that costimulation increased PKC-θ binding to NPCs in primary human T cells (Figure 1E) and in Jurkat T cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PKC-θ deletion results in a decreased ratio of nuclear-to-cytoplasmic importin-β1 in resting T cells.
source: Using confocal microscopy, we found that PKC-θ deletion resulted in a decreased ratio of nuclear-to-cytoplasmic of importin-β1 and Ran (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: PKC-θ deletion results in a decreased ratio of nuclear-to-cytoplasmic Ran in resting T cells.
source: Using confocal microscopy, we found that PKC-θ deletion resulted in a decreased ratio of nuclear-to-cytoplasmic of importin-β1 and Ran (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: PKC-θ deletion results in decreased translocation of importin-β1 and Ran to the nuclear fraction.
source: PKC-θ deletion also resulted in a decreased translocation of importin-β1 and Ran to the nuclear fraction (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation experiments shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In wild-type T cells, importin-β1 constitutively coimmunoprecipitates with NPCs.
source: In wild-type T cells, importin-β1 constitutively coimmunoprecipitated with NPCs, and anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 costimulation significantly increased their association; in contrast, in Prkcq−/− T cells, importin-β1 barely bound to NPCs, regardless of stimulation (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 costimulation significantly increases importin-β1 association with NPCs in wild-type T cells.
source: In wild-type T cells, importin-β1 constitutively coimmunoprecipitated with NPCs, and anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 costimulation significantly increased their association; in contrast, in Prkcq−/− T cells, importin-β1 barely bound to NPCs, regardless of stimulation (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: In Prkcq−/− T cells, importin-β1 barely binds to NPCs, regardless of stimulation.
source: In wild-type T cells, importin-β1 constitutively coimmunoprecipitated with NPCs, and anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 costimulation significantly increased their association; in contrast, in Prkcq−/− T cells, importin-β1 barely bound to NPCs, regardless of stimulation (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: PKC-θ deficiency alters both the basal state and TCR-induced nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
source: These data indicate that PKC-θ deficiency alters both the basal state and TCR-induced nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing effects in both unstimulated and stimulated conditions.

claim: GST-RanGAP1 shows direct interaction with PKC-θ in unstimulated Jurkat cells lysate.
source: Among them, GST-RanGAP1 showed the most obvious association and a direct interaction with PKC-θ in unstimulated Jurkat cells lysate (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PKC-θ weakly interacts constitutively with sumoylated RanGAP1.
source: Reciprocal co-IP from Jurkat T cells showed that PKC-θ weakly interacted constitutively with sumoylated RanGAP1, and costimulation with anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 Abs markedly increased the association of PKC-θ with both forms of RanGAP1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Costimulation with anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 markedly increases the association of PKC-θ with both forms of RanGAP1.
source: Reciprocal co-IP from Jurkat T cells showed that PKC-θ weakly interacted constitutively with sumoylated RanGAP1, and costimulation with anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 Abs markedly increased the association of PKC-θ with both forms of RanGAP1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A significant colocalization of PKC-θ and RanGAP1 in NPCs is observed in Jurkat T cells after anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 or PMA plus Iono stimulation.
source: A significant colocalization of PKC-θ and RanGAP1 in NPCs was also observed in Jurkat T cells after anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 or PMA plus Iono stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: RanGAP1 sumoylation is not required for its interaction with PKC-θ.
source: PKC-θ coimmunoprecipitated efficiently with RanGAP1-K524R (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), implying that RanGAP1 sumoylation is not required for its interaction with PKC-θ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with the non-sumoylatable RanGAP1-K524R mutant shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both the sumoylated and non-sumoylated forms of RanGAP1 interact more strongly with PKC-θ-A148E than with wild-type PKC-θ.
source: Reciprocal IP showed that both the sumoylated and non-sumoylated forms of RanGAP1 interacted more strongly with PKC-θ-A148E than with wild-type PKC-θ, whereas PKC-θ−2KR and PKC-θ-K409R displayed a much weaker interaction, if at all (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: PKC-θ−2KR and PKC-θ-K409R display much weaker interaction with RanGAP1.
source: Reciprocal IP showed that both the sumoylated and non-sumoylated forms of RanGAP1 interacted more strongly with PKC-θ-A148E than with wild-type PKC-θ, whereas PKC-θ−2KR and PKC-θ-K409R displayed a much weaker interaction, if at all (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Wild-type PKC-θ translocates to the NE in response to PMA plus Iono stimulation.
source: Following biochemical isolation of the NE, we observed that wild-type PKC-θ translocated to the NE in response to PMA plus Iono stimulation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), consistent with the results in Figure 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: PKC-θ-A148E is constitutively localized to the NE regardless of stimulation.
source: Interestingly, PKC-θ-A148E was constitutively localized to the NE regardless of stimulation, while no apparent NE localization of either PKC-θ−2KR or PKC-θ-K409R was observed even after PMA plus Iono stimulation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), consistent with the result in Figure 2E.
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: No apparent NE localization of PKC-θ−2KR or PKC-θ-K409R is observed even after PMA plus Iono stimulation.
source: Interestingly, PKC-θ-A148E was constitutively localized to the NE regardless of stimulation, while no apparent NE localization of either PKC-θ−2KR or PKC-θ-K409R was observed even after PMA plus Iono stimulation (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), consistent with the result in Figure 2E.
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Wild-type PKC-θ, but not PKC-θ−2KR, is sumoylated.
source: As expected, wild-type PKC-θ, but not PKC-θ−2KR, was sumoylated (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: PKC-θ-K409R cannot be sumoylated.
source: Interestingly, PKC-θ-K409R, like PKC-θ−2KR, could not be sumoylated, whereas PKC-θ-A148E was sumoylated more strongly than wild-type PKC-θ (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), indicating that the catalytic activity of PKC-θ is required for its sumoylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: PKC-θ-A148E is sumoylated more strongly than wild-type PKC-θ.
source: Interestingly, PKC-θ-K409R, like PKC-θ−2KR, could not be sumoylated, whereas PKC-θ-A148E was sumoylated more strongly than wild-type PKC-θ (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), indicating that the catalytic activity of PKC-θ is required for its sumoylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The catalytic activity of PKC-θ is required for its sumoylation.
source: Interestingly, PKC-θ-K409R, like PKC-θ−2KR, could not be sumoylated, whereas PKC-θ-A148E was sumoylated more strongly than wild-type PKC-θ (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), indicating that the catalytic activity of PKC-θ is required for its sumoylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the kinase-dead mutant PKC-θ-K409R cannot be sumoylated.

claim: PKC-θ sumoylation is required for its NE translocation.
source: Combining the results in Figure 2E–G with the result in Figure 2D, we conclude that PKC-θ sumoylation, rather than the sumoylation of RanGAP1, was important for their association and that PKC-θ sumoylation is required for its NE translocation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations showing that desumoylated PKC-θ mutants do not translocate to the NE.

claim: NE-localized RanGAP1 is decreased in Prkcq−/− T cells, with most RanGAP1 found in the cytosol.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that NE-localized RanGAP1 was decreased in Prkcq−/− T cells, with most RanGAP1 found in the cytosol (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transient knockdown of endogenous PKC-θ in Jurkat T cells increases cytosol-localized RanGAP1 and decreases NE-localized RanGAP1.
source: When we used siPKC-θ to transiently knock down endogenous PKC-θ in Jurkat T cells, the amount of cytosol-localized RanGAP1 increased, while NE-localized RanGAP1 decreased (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Stimulation of human primary T cells with anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 or with PMA plus Iono increases the ratio of sumoylated to unsumoylated RanGAP1.
source: Consistent with this result, stimulation of human primary T cells with anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 or with PMA plus Iono increased the ratio of sumoylated to unsumoylated RanGAP1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TCR plus CD28 costimulation increases the ratio of sumoylated to unsumoylated RanGAP1 in mouse primary T cells and Jurkat T cells, but not when PKC-θ is knocked out or knocked down.
source: A similar increase in this ratio was observed when mouse primary T cells or Jurkat T cells were costimulated with anti-CD3 plus anti-CD28 Abs; however, this increase was not observed when expression of PKC-θ was knocked out or knocked down (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, respectively; whole-cell lysates [WCL]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PKC-θ deficiency decreases the ratio of sumoylated to unsumoylated RanGAP1 in resting cells.
source: Consistently, PKC-θ deficiency also decreased the ratio in resting cells (Figure 3D,E, respectively; WCL and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sumoylated RanGAP1 is largely absent or substantially reduced in PKC-θ-depleted mouse primary peripheral T cells or Jurkat T cells in both resting and activated states.
source: Sumoylated RanGAP1 was present in Mab414 NPC IPs prepared from mouse primary peripheral T cells or Jurkat T cells regardless of stimulation, but was largely absent or substantially reduced when these cells were depleted of PKC-θ both in resting and in activated T cells (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, respectively; IP and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PKC-θ promotes the sumoylation of RanGAP1 as well as the incorporation of RanGAP1 into the NPC both in resting and activated cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that PKC-θ promotes the sumoylation of RanGAP1 as well as the incorporation of RanGAP1 into the NPC both in resting and activated cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing reduced RanGAP1 sumoylation and NPC association in PKC-θ-deficient cells.

claim: In Prkcq−/− mouse thymocytes, TCR plus CD28 costimulation increases the association of RanGAP1 with the NPC.
source: Interestingly, however, and in contrast to peripheral T cells or Jurkat cells, in Prkcq−/− mouse thymocytes, TCR plus CD28 costimulation appeared to increase the association of RanGAP1 with the NPC (Figure 3F; IP) as well as its relative increased sumoylation (Figure 3F; WCL) in a manner that was not affected by PKC-θ deletion, although PKC-θ deficiency did decrease the ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 in resting thymocytes (Figure 3F, WCL), similar to the mature T cells (Figure 3D, WCL).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In Prkcq−/− mouse thymocytes, TCR plus CD28 costimulation increases RanGAP1 sumoylation in a manner not affected by PKC-θ deletion.
source: Interestingly, however, and in contrast to peripheral T cells or Jurkat cells, in Prkcq−/− mouse thymocytes, TCR plus CD28 costimulation appeared to increase the association of RanGAP1 with the NPC (Figure 3F; IP) as well as its relative increased sumoylation (Figure 3F; WCL) in a manner that was not affected by PKC-θ deletion, although PKC-θ deficiency did decrease the ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 in resting thymocytes (Figure 3F, WCL), similar to the mature T cells (Figure 3D, WCL).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PKC-θ deficiency decreases the ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 in resting thymocytes.
source: Interestingly, however, and in contrast to peripheral T cells or Jurkat cells, in Prkcq−/− mouse thymocytes, TCR plus CD28 costimulation appeared to increase the association of RanGAP1 with the NPC (Figure 3F; IP) as well as its relative increased sumoylation (Figure 3F; WCL) in a manner that was not affected by PKC-θ deletion, although PKC-θ deficiency did decrease the ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 in resting thymocytes (Figure 3F, WCL), similar to the mature T cells (Figure 3D, WCL).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Upon TCR stimulation, ERK phosphorylation is decreased in Prkcq−/− mature T cells.
source: Upon TCR stimulation, ERK phosphorylation was decreased in Prkcq−/− mature T cells (Figure 3D, WCL), consistent with the finding that PKC-θ activates ERK via RasGRP1-Ras signaling (Roose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3D and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: The activation of ERK is reduced in Prkcq−/− thymocytes.
source: Notably, the activation of ERK was also reduced in Prkcq−/− thymocytes (Figure 3F, WCL), consistent with a previous report (Morley et al., 2008), but in contrast to another report (Pfeifhofer et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3F and is consistent with one previous report but contrasts with another.

claim: PKC-θ controls constitutive RanGAP1 sumoylation in both resting mature and immature T cells.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that PKC-θ controls constitutive RanGAP1 sumoylation in both resting mature and immature T cells, but is critical for the TCR-induced RanGAP1 sumoylation and RanGAP1-SUMO association with NPCs only in mature T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations comparing mature T cells and thymocytes.

claim: PKC-θ is critical for TCR-induced RanGAP1 sumoylation and RanGAP1-SUMO association with NPCs only in mature T cells.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that PKC-θ controls constitutive RanGAP1 sumoylation in both resting mature and immature T cells, but is critical for the TCR-induced RanGAP1 sumoylation and RanGAP1-SUMO association with NPCs only in mature T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations comparing mature T cells and thymocytes.

claim: PKC-θ deficiency does not affect TCR-induced phosphorylation of JNK and c-Jun in either mouse splenic T cells or thymocytes.
source: Whereas PKC-θ deficiency did not affect TCR-induced phosphorylation of JNK and c-Jun (indicative of its activation) in either mouse splenic T cells or thymocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), confocal microscopy and nuclear fractionation showed that the TCR-induced nuclear localization of c-Jun was blocked in Prkcq−/− splenic T cells (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), but remained intact in Prkcq−/− thymocytes (Figure 3I,J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that PKC-θ regulates the nuclear import of c-Jun through the NPC in mature T cells, but not in thymocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: TCR-induced nuclear localization of c-Jun is blocked in Prkcq−/− splenic T cells.
source: Whereas PKC-θ deficiency did not affect TCR-induced phosphorylation of JNK and c-Jun (indicative of its activation) in either mouse splenic T cells or thymocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), confocal microscopy and nuclear fractionation showed that the TCR-induced nuclear localization of c-Jun was blocked in Prkcq−/− splenic T cells (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), but remained intact in Prkcq−/− thymocytes (Figure 3I,J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that PKC-θ regulates the nuclear import of c-Jun through the NPC in mature T cells, but not in thymocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and nuclear fractionation shown in Figure 3G,H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TCR-induced nuclear localization of c-Jun remains intact in Prkcq−/− thymocytes.
source: Whereas PKC-θ deficiency did not affect TCR-induced phosphorylation of JNK and c-Jun (indicative of its activation) in either mouse splenic T cells or thymocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), confocal microscopy and nuclear fractionation showed that the TCR-induced nuclear localization of c-Jun was blocked in Prkcq−/− splenic T cells (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), but remained intact in Prkcq−/− thymocytes (Figure 3I,J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that PKC-θ regulates the nuclear import of c-Jun through the NPC in mature T cells, but not in thymocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and nuclear fractionation shown in Figure 3I,J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PKC-θ regulates the nuclear import of c-Jun through the NPC in mature T cells, but not in thymocytes.
source: Whereas PKC-θ deficiency did not affect TCR-induced phosphorylation of JNK and c-Jun (indicative of its activation) in either mouse splenic T cells or thymocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), confocal microscopy and nuclear fractionation showed that the TCR-induced nuclear localization of c-Jun was blocked in Prkcq−/− splenic T cells (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), but remained intact in Prkcq−/− thymocytes (Figure 3I,J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that PKC-θ regulates the nuclear import of c-Jun through the NPC in mature T cells, but not in thymocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of PKC-θ deficiency on c-Jun nuclear localization in mature T cells versus thymocytes.

claim: After 12 hr stimulation, PKC-θ deletion-induced defects in RanGAP1 sumoylation and its binding to NPCs and c-Jun nuclear translocation still remain.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H, after 12 hr stimulation, PKC-θ deletion-induced defects in RanGAP1 sumoylation and its binding to NPCs and c-Jun nuclear translocation still remain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and subcellular fractionation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: PKC-θ may promote c-Jun nuclear import, but not its phosphorylation per se.
source: Thus, PKC-θ may promote c-Jun nuclear import, but not its phosphorylation per se, suggesting that it regulates AP-1 activation primarily by controlling the function of the NPC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PKC-θ deficiency blocks c-Jun nuclear import but not its phosphorylation.

claim: PKC-θ regulates AP-1 activation primarily by controlling the function of the NPC.
source: Thus, PKC-θ may promote c-Jun nuclear import, but not its phosphorylation per se, suggesting that it regulates AP-1 activation primarily by controlling the function of the NPC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing that PKC-θ affects nuclear import but not phosphorylation of c-Jun.

claim: TCR plus CD28 costimulation increases phosphorylation of RanGAP1 in control Jurkat T cells, but not in PKC-θ knockdown cells.
source: Using a mixture of phospho-Ser- and phospho-Thr-specific antibodies, we found that TCR plus CD28 costimulation increased phosphorylation of RanGAP1 in control Jurkat T cells, but not in PKC-θ knockdown cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PKC-θ immunoprecipitated from Jurkat T cells efficiently phosphorylates RanGAP1 in vitro.
source: Furthermore, an in vitro kinase assay demonstrated that PKC-θ immunoprecipitated from Jurkat T cells efficiently phosphorylated RanGAP1 (Figure 4B), indicating that RanGAP1 is most likely a direct PKC-θ substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by an in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RanGAP1 is most likely a direct PKC-θ substrate.
source: Furthermore, an in vitro kinase assay demonstrated that PKC-θ immunoprecipitated from Jurkat T cells efficiently phosphorylated RanGAP1 (Figure 4B), indicating that RanGAP1 is most likely a direct PKC-θ substrate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro kinase assay showing direct phosphorylation of RanGAP1 by PKC-θ.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified five potential phosphorylation serine or threonine sites on RanGAP1.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of PKC-θ-phosphorylated RanGAP1 identified five potential phosphorylation serine or threonine sites on RanGAP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mutation of both Ser504 and Ser506 reduces the phosphorylation of RanGAP1.
source: Upon mutating each of these residues individually to alanine, we found that mutation both Ser504 and Ser506, but not the three other residues, reduced the phosphorylation of RanGAP1, while phosphorylation of the double mutant S504A/S506A (RanGAP1AA) was significantly decreased (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis of mutant RanGAP1 proteins shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Phosphorylation of the double mutant S504A/S506A (RanGAP1AA) is significantly decreased.
source: Upon mutating each of these residues individually to alanine, we found that mutation both Ser504 and Ser506, but not the three other residues, reduced the phosphorylation of RanGAP1, while phosphorylation of the double mutant S504A/S506A (RanGAP1AA) was significantly decreased (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PKC-θ phosphorylates truncated GST-RanGAP1431-587 but not the S504A/S506A double mutant in vitro.
source: In the in vitro kinase assay, we detected phosphorylation of truncated GST-RanGAP1431-587 but not the S504A/S506A double mutant (RanGAP1AA; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by an in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: S504 (10/11) and S506 (8/11) sites and three adjacent serines are conserved across different species.
source: Sequence alignment of RanGAP1 from different species showed that S504 (10/11) and S506 (8/11) sites and three adjacent serines are conserved (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A mouse RanGAP1 fragment containing conserved sites is phosphorylated by PKC-θ in an in vitro kinase assay.
source: A mouse RanGAP1 fragment containing these conserved sites was also phosphorylated by PKC-θ in an in vitro kinase assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by an in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 is significantly decreased in cells expressing the S504A mutant or the double mutant RanGAP1AA.
source: When we calculated the ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 in the mutant cells, we observed that this ratio was significantly decreased in cells expressing the S504A mutant or the double mutant RanGAP1AA and, to a lesser extent, in S506A-expressing cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 is decreased to a lesser extent in S506A-expressing cells.
source: When we calculated the ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 in the mutant cells, we observed that this ratio was significantly decreased in cells expressing the S504A mutant or the double mutant RanGAP1AA and, to a lesser extent, in S506A-expressing cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of RanGAP1, particularly on Ser504, promotes its sumoylation.
source: Together, these findings suggest that PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of RanGAP1, particularly on Ser504, promotes its sumoylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing that mutation of Ser504 significantly reduces RanGAP1 sumoylation.

claim: A non-sumoylated RanGAP1 mutant (K524R) is capable of associating with Ubc9.
source: Hence, we first examined whether RanGAP1 sumoylation affects its binding to Ubc9 and found that a non-sumoylated RanGAP1 mutant (K524R) was still capable of associating with Ubc9 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HA-RanGAP1AA-K524R shows a decreased association with Ubc9 compared with HA-RanGAP1-K524R.
source: We then analyzed the association of these mutants with Ubc9 by reciprocal co-IP and found that, compared with HA-RanGAP1-K524R, HA-RanGAP1AA-K524R showed a decreased association with Ubc9, while HA-RanGAP1EE-K524R had a stronger interaction (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: HA-RanGAP1EE-K524R has a stronger interaction with Ubc9 compared with HA-RanGAP1-K524R.
source: We then analyzed the association of these mutants with Ubc9 by reciprocal co-IP and found that, compared with HA-RanGAP1-K524R, HA-RanGAP1AA-K524R showed a decreased association with Ubc9, while HA-RanGAP1EE-K524R had a stronger interaction (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: RanGAP1 phosphorylation promotes its binding to Ubc9.
source: This result indicates that RanGAP1 phosphorylation promotes its binding to Ubc9 and provides an explanation for our finding that mutation of the RanGAP1 PKC-θ phosphorylation sites inhibits its sumoylation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing differential binding of phospho-mimetic and non-phosphorylatable mutants to Ubc9.

claim: HA-RanGAP1AA binds to Ubc9 and RanBP2 less effectively than non-mutated HA-RanGAP1.
source: HA-RanGAP1AA bound to Ubc9 and RanBP2 less effectively than non-mutated HA-RanGAP1; in contrast, HA-RanGAP1EE bound more effectively to Ubc9 and RanBP2 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: HA-RanGAP1EE binds more effectively to Ubc9 and RanBP2 than non-mutated HA-RanGAP1.
source: HA-RanGAP1AA bound to Ubc9 and RanBP2 less effectively than non-mutated HA-RanGAP1; in contrast, HA-RanGAP1EE bound more effectively to Ubc9 and RanBP2 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The RanGAP1EE mutant protein displays an increased ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 relative to the two other RanGAP1 proteins.
source: As expected, due to its stronger association with Ubc9, the RanGAP1EE mutant protein displayed an increased ratio of RanGAP1-SUMO1 to RanGAP1 relative to the two other RanGAP1 proteins (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis and quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of RanGAP1 is essential for assembly of the RanBP2/RanGAP1-SUMO1/Ubc9 subcomplex in NPCs.
source: These results reveal that PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of RanGAP1 is essential for assembly of the RanBP2/RanGAP1-SUMO1/Ubc9 subcomplex in NPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing that phosphorylation promotes RanGAP1 binding to Ubc9 and RanBP2.

claim: Replacement of the two PKC-θ phosphorylation sites in RanGAP1 by glutamic acid (S504E/S506E) increases the overall structural stability of RanGAP1.
source: Intriguingly, in silico analysis showed that replacement of the two PKC-θ phosphorylation sites in RanGAP1 by glutamic acid (S504E/S506E) increased the overall structural stability of RanGAP1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B); this increased stability likely contributed to the observed increased association between RanGAP1 and Ubc9.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in silico analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increased structural stability of RanGAP1EE likely contributes to the observed increased association between RanGAP1 and Ubc9.
source: Intriguingly, in silico analysis showed that replacement of the two PKC-θ phosphorylation sites in RanGAP1 by glutamic acid (S504E/S506E) increased the overall structural stability of RanGAP1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B); this increased stability likely contributed to the observed increased association between RanGAP1 and Ubc9.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in silico analysis and the experimental observations.

claim: PKC-θ phosphorylates RanGAP1 to increase its association with Ubc9 and, in turn, the sumoylation of RanGAP1, thereby facilitating assembly of the RanBP2/RanGAP1-SUMO1/Ubc9 subcomplex upon TCR stimulation.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PKC-θ phosphorylates RanGAP1 to increase its association with Ubc9 and, in turn, the sumoylation of RanGAP1, thereby facilitating assembly of the RanBP2/RanGAP1-SUMO1/Ubc9 subcomplex upon TCR stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental observations in this section.

claim: Expression of RanGAP1 mutant with decreased RanGAP1 protein level results in blocked TCR-induced nuclear translocation of NFATc1, p65, and c-Jun and c-Fos.
source: We confirmed that expression of this mutant resulted in blocked TCR-induced nuclear translocation of NFATc1, p65 (NF-κB), and c-Jun and c-Fos (AP-1) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The defective nuclear translocation of NFATc1, p65, and AP-1 in RanGAP1-KD cells is largely rescued by wild-type RanGAP1, but not by the RanGAP1AA mutant.
source: Using subcellular fractionation (Figure 6A) or confocal microscopy (Figure 6B,C), we observed that the defective nuclear translocation of these transcription factors in RanGAP1-KD cells was largely rescued by wild-type RanGAP1, but not by the RanGAP1AA mutant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6A,B,C.

claim: Stimulated RanGAP1-KD cells display reduced IL-2 production compared to control cells.
source: Similarly, while stimulated RanGAP1-KD cells displayed reduced IL-2 production, which is known to require the cooperative activity of the above transcription factors, as compared to control cells, transfection with wild-type RanGAP1 rescued IL-2 production, while RanGAP1AA did not (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Transfection with wild-type RanGAP1 rescues IL-2 production in RanGAP1-KD cells, while RanGAP1AA does not.
source: Similarly, while stimulated RanGAP1-KD cells displayed reduced IL-2 production, which is known to require the cooperative activity of the above transcription factors, as compared to control cells, transfection with wild-type RanGAP1 rescued IL-2 production, while RanGAP1AA did not (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In resting T cells, PKC-θ knockdown leads to reduced nuclear import of Dis3, RPS3, and RPL26.
source: In resting T cells, PKC-θ knockdown led to reduced nuclear import of Dis3, RPS3, and RPL26, as well as impaired nuclear export of CRM1, consistent with their requirement for importin-β1 or the Ran system; however, the Ran-independent NXF1 also displayed impaired nuclear export (i.e., nuclear retention) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: In resting T cells, PKC-θ knockdown leads to impaired nuclear export of CRM1.
source: In resting T cells, PKC-θ knockdown led to reduced nuclear import of Dis3, RPS3, and RPL26, as well as impaired nuclear export of CRM1, consistent with their requirement for importin-β1 or the Ran system; however, the Ran-independent NXF1 also displayed impaired nuclear export (i.e., nuclear retention) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: In resting T cells, the Ran-independent NXF1 displays impaired nuclear export (nuclear retention) upon PKC-θ knockdown.
source: In resting T cells, PKC-θ knockdown led to reduced nuclear import of Dis3, RPS3, and RPL26, as well as impaired nuclear export of CRM1, consistent with their requirement for importin-β1 or the Ran system; however, the Ran-independent NXF1 also displayed impaired nuclear export (i.e., nuclear retention) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: In TCR-activated cells, PKC-θ knockdown does not affect the nuclear transport of CRM1, Dis3, RPS3, or RPL26.
source: In TCR-activated cells, PKC-θ knockdown did not affect the nuclear transport of CRM1, Dis3, RPS3, or RPL26 (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: TCR stimulation does not alleviate siPKC-θ-caused defects in importin-β1 nuclear import.
source: However, TCR stimulation did not alleviate siPKC-θ-caused defects in importin-β1 nuclear import and in NXF1 nuclear export.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing persistent defects after TCR stimulation.

claim: TCR stimulation does not alleviate siPKC-θ-caused defects in NXF1 nuclear export.
source: However, TCR stimulation did not alleviate siPKC-θ-caused defects in importin-β1 nuclear import and in NXF1 nuclear export.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing persistent defects after TCR stimulation.

claim: Independent of the stimulation status, PKC-θ knockdown does not affect the nuclear transport of histones.
source: Interestingly, independent of the stimulation status, PKC-θ knockdown did not affect the nuclear transport of histones, nor did it affect the nuclear import of stimulation-induced p53.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no effect on histone transport.

claim: PKC-θ knockdown does not affect the nuclear import of stimulation-induced p53.
source: Interestingly, independent of the stimulation status, PKC-θ knockdown did not affect the nuclear transport of histones, nor did it affect the nuclear import of stimulation-induced p53.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no effect on p53 nuclear import.

claim: Neither PKC-θ nor TCR signaling regulates histones transport.
source: In summary, neither PKC-θ nor TCR signaling regulates histones transport; in resting T cells, the importin-β1- or Ran-dependent nuclear transport pathways we tested, with the exception of histones, are dependent on PKC-θ; in activated cells, PKC-θ was dispensable for their nuclear transport, except for the nuclear transport of importin-β1; and PKC-θ was required for NXF1 transport under both statuses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: In resting T cells, the importin-β1- or Ran-dependent nuclear transport pathways tested (with the exception of histones) are dependent on PKC-θ.
source: In summary, neither PKC-θ nor TCR signaling regulates histones transport; in resting T cells, the importin-β1- or Ran-dependent nuclear transport pathways we tested, with the exception of histones, are dependent on PKC-θ; in activated cells, PKC-θ was dispensable for their nuclear transport, except for the nuclear transport of importin-β1; and PKC-θ was required for NXF1 transport under both statuses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: In activated cells, PKC-θ is dispensable for nuclear transport of Dis3, RPS3, RPL26, and CRM1, except for the nuclear transport of importin-β1.
source: In summary, neither PKC-θ nor TCR signaling regulates histones transport; in resting T cells, the importin-β1- or Ran-dependent nuclear transport pathways we tested, with the exception of histones, are dependent on PKC-θ; in activated cells, PKC-θ was dispensable for their nuclear transport, except for the nuclear transport of importin-β1; and PKC-θ was required for NXF1 transport under both statuses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: PKC-θ is required for NXF1 transport under both resting and activated statuses.
source: In summary, neither PKC-θ nor TCR signaling regulates histones transport; in resting T cells, the importin-β1- or Ran-dependent nuclear transport pathways we tested, with the exception of histones, are dependent on PKC-θ; in activated cells, PKC-θ was dispensable for their nuclear transport, except for the nuclear transport of importin-β1; and PKC-θ was required for NXF1 transport under both statuses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: PKC-θ-RanGAP signaling axis is differentially required in various nuclear transport pathways.
source: Therefore, PKC-θ-RanGAP signaling axis is differentially required in various nuclear transport pathways.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing differential effects on different transport pathways.

claim: The nuclear import of importin-β1 is partially rescued by RanGAP1EE both before and after TCR stimulation in siPKC-θ T cells.
source: As expected, the nuclear import of importin-β1 was partially rescued by RanGAP1EE both before or after TCR stimulation in siPKC-θ T cells (Figure 8A), consistent with our results that PKC-θ is required for RanGAP1 SUMOylation in both states (Figures 1G–L and 3D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: RanGAP1EE mutant rescues TCR-induced nuclear translocation of c-Jun in siPKC-θ Jurkat T cells.
source: Moreover, in contrast to RanGAP1AA mutant, RanGAP1EE mutant did rescue TCR-induced nuclear translocation of c-Jun in siPKC-θ Jurkat T cells (Figure 8A) or in Prkcq−/− primary T cells (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis and confocal microscopy shown in Figure 8A,B,C.

claim: RanGAP1EE mutant rescues TCR-induced nuclear translocation of c-Jun in Prkcq−/− primary T cells.
source: Moreover, in contrast to RanGAP1AA mutant, RanGAP1EE mutant did rescue TCR-induced nuclear translocation of c-Jun in siPKC-θ Jurkat T cells (Figure 8A) or in Prkcq−/− primary T cells (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: NFATc1 or p65 nuclear import is not rescued by the RanGAP1EE mutant in PKC-θ-deficient T cells.
source: As expected, NFATc1 or p65 nuclear import was not rescued by the RanGAP1EE mutant, consistent with the fact that TCR-proximal upstream signaling pathways are also disrupted in PKC-θ-deficient T cells (Pfeifhofer et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: siPKC-θ-induced nuclear retention of NXF1 is reversed by forced RanGAP1EE expression.
source: As to the mRNA export receptor NXF1, siPKC-θ-induced nuclear retention (Figure 7) was reversed by forced RanGAP1EE expression (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Formation of the RanBP2 subcomplex is the key step downstream of PKC-θ signaling that regulates the nuclear transport of transcription factors, especially c-Jun.
source: Thus, we conclude that formation of the RanBP2 subcomplex is the key step downstream of PKC-θ signaling that regulates the nuclear transport of transcription factors, especially c-Jun.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments showing that RanGAP1EE can restore c-Jun nuclear import.

claim: Upon TCR plus CD28 costimulation, PKC-θ phosphorylates RanGAP1 to promote its interaction with Ubc9 and increase the sumoylation of RanGAP1.
source: Here, we have demonstrated that upon TCR plus CD28 costimulation, PKC-θ phosphorylates RanGAP1 to promote its interaction with Ubc9 and increase the sumoylation of RanGAP1, which, in turn, enhances assembly of the RanBP2 subcomplex and, thus, directly promotes the nuclear import of AP-1, NFAT, and NF-κB (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of RanGAP1 enhances assembly of the RanBP2 subcomplex and directly promotes the nuclear import of AP-1, NFAT, and NF-κB.
source: Here, we have demonstrated that upon TCR plus CD28 costimulation, PKC-θ phosphorylates RanGAP1 to promote its interaction with Ubc9 and increase the sumoylation of RanGAP1, which, in turn, enhances assembly of the RanBP2 subcomplex and, thus, directly promotes the nuclear import of AP-1, NFAT, and NF-κB (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: This work reveals a novel signaling axis, TCR-PKC-θ-RanGAP1, which regulates T-cell activation via control of nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
source: Thus, our work reveals a novel signaling axis, TCR-PKC-θ-RanGAP1, which regulates T-cell activation via control of nucleo-cytoplasmic transport, thereby linking TCR signaling to formation of the NPC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main contribution.

claim: The TCR-PKC-θ-RanGAP1 signaling axis links TCR signaling to formation of the NPC.
source: Thus, our work reveals a novel signaling axis, TCR-PKC-θ-RanGAP1, which regulates T-cell activation via control of nucleo-cytoplasmic transport, thereby linking TCR signaling to formation of the NPC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main contribution.
